<reason>Side B won decisively on every major clash. On the central legal question, Side B showed that once schools directly share revenue, unilateral pay caps and transfer rules violate antitrust law—and that lawsuit settlements like the House framework cannot bind incoming recruits who were never party to the case. Cornered by this pressure question in Rebuttal 2, Side A had to pivot to wishing for a Congressional antitrust exemption, which Side B rightly exposed in Closing as a retreat outside the motion's compliance framework that seeks federal permission to cap athlete pay without athlete consent (a point Side A then bizarrely misattributed to Side B in A5.1). Side B also effectively neutralized Side A's tax scare by pointing out that unionized graduate assistants at private universities already receive $60,000 tax-exempt tuition waivers while bargaining over taxable stipends, and turned Side A's complaints about workers' compensation and arbitration over "managing roster depth" into a compelling indictment of paternalistic school governance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's pressure question [B3.1] and closing follow-up [B5.1] on the House settlement: by pointing out that a lawsuit settlement cannot waive antitrust rights for future recruits who never signed it, Side B forced Side A to abandon ad hoc compliance in [A4.1] and plead for a Congressional antitrust exemption, which Side B then framed as asking Congress to let billion-dollar programs collude to cap player pay without player consent.</best_rebuttal>
